item.title: Can we better identify which cows benefit from intrauterine treatment with cephapirin?
item.description:
This project needs a master’s student (M.Sc.) in veterinary science. If you have a background in veterinary medicine or animal science and experience in handling cattle, please contact us!

The objective of this study is to identify the impact of intrauterine cephalosporin on the reproductive success of cows with uterine infections.

Team

  • José Denis-Robichaud (principal investigator)
  • Marcio Costa (collaborator)
  • Hélène Lardé (collaborator)
  • Isabella Nicola (collaborator)
  • Marie-Lou Gauthier (collaborator)

In brief

After 21 days in milk (DIM), the most commonly studied reproductive conditions in dairy cows are purulent vaginal discharge (PVD) and endometritis, as they are associated with impaired reproductive performance. Although in both cases the diagnosis is made by measuring inflammation, intrauterine treatment with cephapirin (CEPH; Metricure, Merck Animal Health) has been shown to have a positive impact on the reproductive success of affected cows. However, the sensitivity of these tests in identifying uterine infection has recently been suggested to be low, while another diagnostic tool that can be used on the farm, the luminometer, has been shown to have better sensitivity. The main objective of this randomized controlled trial is therefore to identify the impact of CEPH on the reproductive success of cows with EVP, endometritis, and/or uterine infection. The secondary objective is to use an economic analysis to determine in which context(s) the implementation of a systematic approach to diagnosis and treatment would be financially beneficial for dairy farmers. This study will identify whether a subpopulation of cows with EVP and/or endometritis, i.e., those with uterine infection, benefit from CEPH, while those with inflammation only, i.e., without infection, do not need this treatment. This project is part of a vision for the judicious use of antimicrobials by improving the identification of cows with uterine infections. In addition, the economic analysis could support better adoption of treatment for affected cows, thereby improving the health of dairy herds.

item.title: Use of bacterial markers to predict endometritis in dairy cows
item.description:
This project needs a Master’s degree (M.Sc.) student in veterinary science. If you have a background in veterinary medicine, animal science, molecular biology, bioinformatics, or a related field, and you have experience in research laboratories and working with cattle, please contact us!

This study aims to detect bacterial markers present in the uterus of dairy cows that can predict the onset of endometritis.

Team

  • Marcio Costa (principal investigator)
  • Hélène Lardé (collaborator)
  • Isabella Nicola (collaborator)
  • José Denis-Robichaud (collaborator)

In brief

Endometritis, an inflammation of the inner lining of the uterus, is common in dairy cows, particularly in the postpartum period. It affects fertility and overall health, resulting in significant economic losses in the dairy industry. The significant consequences of endometritis include longer intervals between pregnancies, increased need for veterinary care, and use of antimicrobials, which are associated with decreased performance. Nearly 100% of cows have bacterial contamination in the uterus after calving, and expected changes in the microbiota are observed during uterine involution. However, when there are imbalances in the resident bacteria, the environment becomes more susceptible to the proliferation of pathogenic organisms, such as Trueperella and E. coli. New DNA sequencing and quantification technologies have become readily available in recent decades, enabling exponential growth in our understanding of the relationship between the host and its microbiota. Therefore, this study aims to detect bacterial markers present in the uterus of dairy cows that can predict the onset of endometritis.

Funding

MAPAQ/Ministère de l’Agriculture, des Pêcheries et de l’Alimentation
